strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored CL/NLP problem: token-level recognition of semantic differences in naturally occurring cross-lingual documents.

SwissGov-RSD is potentially valuable: it contains 224 multi-parallel government documents across three language pairs, long inputs, naturally occurring discrepancies, span-level severity labels, detailed annotation guidelines, and documented annotator qualifications and compensation.

The empirical study covers a broad and relevant range of approaches, including unsupervised alignment, multilingual encoders, prompted LLMs, fine-tuned models, and projected-label training. Comparing these systems with iSTS-RSD provides useful evidence that existing synthetic evaluations substantially underestimate real-world difficulty.

The authors report agreement statistics rather than concealing annotation variability, include per-annotator sensitivity results, analyze malformed LLM outputs and document position, and provide prompts, dataset statistics, hyperparameters, and computational timing information.

The main descriptive result is consistent across models and language pairs: correlations on SwissGov-RSD are low, while unsupervised alignment methods are comparatively robust. This establishes a meaningful challenge for future work.
weaknesses: The principal concern is benchmark reliability. Most documents receive only one annotation, while the 25 doubly annotated documents per language pair exhibit low span agreement. EN-DE is particularly problematic: annotators identify 348 versus 75 spans, with token-level F1 around 17–18%. Correlations computed only over matched spans do not address this disagreement about which differences exist and can substantially overstate annotation quality.

The resolution of overlapping annotations is subjective: the authors manually select the annotation that better follows the guidelines and resembles other annotators' label distributions, rather than adjudicating individual disagreements or producing consensus labels. Consequently, the benchmark gold standard may encode annotator-specific coverage and span-boundary preferences, potentially affecting both absolute scores and system rankings. Appendix A.4 acknowledges ranking instability but compares largely different document subsets, so it does not establish robustness.

The central causal interpretation is stronger than the evidence supports. iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD differ simultaneously in domain, document length, difference prevalence, annotation process, source naturalness, and potentially label semantics. The observed performance gap demonstrates poor transfer between these datasets, but does not isolate synthetic augmentation as the cause or show specifically that augmentation “fails to imitate real-world scenarios.” Controlled comparisons matching length, domain, and label distribution are needed.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or document-level bootstrap intervals. This matters because there are only 224 underlying multi-parallel documents, the same English documents recur across language-pair evaluations, correlations are low, and the appendix itself indicates appreciable sensitivity to annotator choice.

Several scoring details are insufficiently specified. The LLM prompt uses a similarity scale where 5 denotes equivalence and -1 denotes punctuation, whereas SwissGov gold labels use 0 for equivalence and 1–5 for difference; the exact transformation and treatment of punctuation and out-of-range predictions are not clearly defined. It is also unclear whether reported correlations pool all tokens globally or aggregate document-level scores.

Padding or truncating malformed LLM outputs may systematically assign errors to document endings. Together with unspecified generation limits, this confounds the claimed long-context degradation and the positional analysis. A constrained output method, chunked evaluation, or explicit ablation of output-length failures would be more informative.

Important reproducibility details remain missing or ambiguous, including crawl dates and snapshotting of mutable web pages, exact HTML extraction and tokenization procedures, document sampling, handling of overlength inputs for 512-token DiffAlign encoders, random seeds, and variability across fine-tuning runs. The paper claims public code and data, but the anonymized manuscript does not permit verification, and redistribution constraints for copyrighted source text may affect long-term reproducibility.

There are presentation and consistency errors that should be corrected, including reporting 886 texts for 224 documents in four languages (which should be 896 absent missing versions) and implausible parameter counts such as 500B for LaBSE and 685B for gte-multilingual-base. These do not overturn the contribution but weaken confidence in experimental documentation.

Overall, the resource is promising and relevant, but the low and uneven annotation agreement prevents a clear Findings recommendation in its current form. Stronger adjudication or additional annotations, reliability-aware evaluation, uncertainty reporting, and a more cautious or controlled synthetic-versus-natural claim could plausibly raise the paper to Findings.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a relevant, underexplored NLP problem and contributes a naturalistic cross-lingual, document-level resource rather than another sentence-level synthetic benchmark. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/3821086f781a411598f28a81f9de87e2/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
SwissGov-RSD contains 224 multi-parallel documents, substantial token volume, three language pairs, naturally occurring additions and omissions, and potentially useful span-level severity labels.

The evaluation covers diverse model families and settings, including unsupervised alignment, prompted and fine-tuned LLMs, and fine-tuned encoders. Reporting both Spearman and Kendall correlations is helpful.

The paper is generally clear and unusually candid about annotation disagreement, output-format failures, language limitations, and computational constraints. Annotation instructions and several implementation details are included.
weaknesses: The benchmark's gold-standard reliability is inadequate for the central contribution. On the shared documents, annotator F1 is only 17–18 for EN–DE, 33–40 for EN–FR, and 44–56 for EN–IT; IoU is even lower. EN–DE annotators mark 348 versus 75 spans and 2,543 versus 839 tokens. These are fundamental disagreements about which differences exist, not merely small boundary variations.

Most documents receive only one annotation. For overlapping documents, the authors manually choose one annotator's version according to guideline adherence and similarity to other annotators' label distributions, rather than adjudicating individual cases or retaining multiple judgments. This subjective selection can suppress legitimate variation and does not produce a defensible gold standard.

High severity-label correlations are calculated only for spans on which annotators already agree sufficiently. They therefore do not compensate for the much larger disagreement in detecting spans. The paper overinterprets these conditional correlations as evidence of improved consistency.

The annotator-sensitivity analysis does not resolve the reliability problem: Table 7 largely compares different document subsets, confounding annotator behavior with document difficulty. The shared 25 documents should instead support paired model evaluations against both annotations, adjudication, and ranking-stability or confidence analyses.

The central synthetic-versus-naturalistic conclusion is heavily confounded. The datasets differ simultaneously in domain, document length, class balance, annotation reliability, and—in the cross-lingual iSTS test—availability of labels on both sides. Consequently, the reported performance drop does not by itself establish that synthetic augmentation is the cause of poor generalization.

Important evaluation details are underspecified. The paper does not clearly explain conversion between similarity-oriented LLM prompts and difference-oriented SwissGov labels, mapping subword predictions to whitespace-token annotations, aggregation of correlations across documents and sides, handling of undefined correlations, or treatment of punctuation. These omissions impede reproduction and could materially affect results.

The sole main metric is dominated by tied zero labels, and no uncertainty intervals, significance tests, span-detection metrics, severity-conditioned results, or robust model-ranking analysis are provided. Padding or truncating malformed LLM outputs is also an arbitrary evaluation choice whose effect is not quantified.

The experimental comparison is incomplete: only selected LLMs are run on SwissGov-RSD, proprietary API settings and version dates are insufficiently controlled, and run-to-run variation or random seeds are not reported. Several model-table metadata entries also appear erroneous, such as LaBSE listed as 500B parameters and gte-multilingual-base as 685B.

The resource is promising, but acceptance in Findings requires sound and reproducible evidence. A revision should obtain multiple annotations or systematic adjudication for the evaluation set, define an uncertainty-aware gold representation, fully specify preprocessing and scoring, and rerun controlled evaluations with paired reliability analyses. These are important but plausibly achievable revisions for a future cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP problem: token-level recognition of semantic differences between long, cross-lingual documents. The naturalistic government-document setting is substantially more realistic than sentence-level synthetic benchmarks.

SwissGov-RSD is a potentially valuable resource: 224 multi-parallel documents covering EN–DE, EN–FR, and EN–IT, with detailed span annotations, extensive guidelines, corpus statistics, and transparent reporting of annotator disagreement and compensation.

The empirical study covers a useful range of approaches, including unsupervised alignment, encoder regression, prompted LLMs, supervised fine-tuning, and projected multilingual labels. Comparing the same methods on iSTS-RSD and SwissGov-RSD clearly demonstrates a large empirical distribution gap.

The finding that simple unsupervised alignment is more robust than specialized or prompted systems on naturalistic documents is useful and supported across three language pairs. The paper also analyzes output failures, token position, efficiency, and an alternative rank-correlation metric.
The manuscript is clearly organized, candid about limitations, relevant to ACL, and includes prompts, annotation instructions, model settings, and supplementary results that facilitate reproduction.
weaknesses: The principal concern is the reliability of the benchmark labels. Each non-overlap document is annotated by only one person, while agreement on the 25 shared documents is very low: token F1 is only about 17–18 for EN–DE, 33–40 for EN–FR, and 44–56 for EN–IT; EN–DE annotators mark 348 versus 75 spans. This is particularly serious because the dataset itself is the central contribution.

The reported high label correlations do not resolve the reliability problem: they exclude unannotated tokens and evaluate only spans already matched between annotators. The paper should report human–human agreement using exactly the primary evaluation protocol—token-level Spearman and Kendall over all tokens—and preferably provide multiply annotated or adjudicated test data.

For overlapping documents, the authors manually select whichever complete annotation better follows the guidelines and other annotators’ label distributions rather than adjudicating individual differences. This subjective selection procedure is insufficiently reproducible and may suppress genuine ambiguity.

Consequently, the central interpretation that naturalistic RSD is intrinsically much harder than synthetic RSD is confounded by annotation noise, domain, document length, class prevalence, and aggregation. The observed performance drop is clear, but the experiments do not isolate its cause; low model–gold correlations may partly reflect an unstable gold standard.

Evaluation relies mainly on a pooled token-level rank correlation with many zero labels. The paper does not provide per-document aggregation, uncertainty intervals, significance tests, or span-detection metrics, making model rankings and cross-dataset comparisons difficult to assess. Appendix results also show large annotator-associated ranking changes, but those subsets mostly contain different documents and therefore do not cleanly measure annotator effects.

The relationship between the reversed SwissGov difference scale and the similarity scale used in the LLM prompts is not specified rigorously. The prompts assign 5 to equivalence and 0 to no relation, whereas SwissGov uses 0 for equivalence and 5 for maximal difference; the transformation applied before correlation must be stated explicitly for reproducibility.

Several broad conclusions overreach the evidence. Not all evaluated LLMs are run on SwissGov-RSD, and the strongest prompted reasoning model on iSTS-RSD is omitted there. Claims about LLM limitations and synthetic augmentation failure should therefore be qualified.

The release claim needs clarification because only labels are CC BY while source texts retain external copyright, and the manuscript contains anonymized/blank code and data links. Stable document identifiers, reconstruction scripts, frozen text where legally permitted, and exact model/API versions are needed for durable reproduction.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP problem with a potentially valuable resource: naturally occurring, document-level semantic differences across English–German, English–French, and English–Italian government texts.

The dataset is substantially more realistic than prior sentence-level or synthetically concatenated benchmarks. The paper provides detailed annotation guidelines, annotator qualifications and compensation, overlap statistics, examples, and an analysis of annotator discrepancies.

The experimental coverage is broad, including unsupervised alignment methods, long-context multilingual encoders, prompted LLMs, fine-tuned models, and projected-label training. The consistent performance drop across languages and model families is useful evidence that the proposed benchmark exposes limitations not visible on iSTS-RSD.

The appendices add useful robustness and diagnostic information, including Kendall correlations, output-format failure rates, positional analysis, label-projection auditing, and inference-time comparisons.
weaknesses: The reliability of the benchmark gold labels is the main concern. Most document pairs receive only one annotation, while the 25-document overlap sets show low span agreement (token F1 approximately 33–56) and only moderate token-level Spearman agreement (43.61–65.09). Overlapping annotations are not adjudicated into consensus labels; instead, one annotation is manually selected partly according to its consistency with other annotators' label distributions. This leaves substantial uncertainty about span completeness, label calibration, and fine-grained model rankings.

The central interpretation overreaches the experimental design. SwissGov-RSD and iSTS-RSD differ simultaneously in naturalness, domain, document length, label prevalence, annotation procedure, and which sides receive labels. Therefore, the observed performance gap does not by itself establish that synthetic augmentation is the cause of poor generalization. Controlled comparisons matched for length, domain, and class distribution are needed.

Evaluation relies primarily on a pooled token-level Spearman correlation, but the aggregation procedure is not fully specified and uncertainty is not reported. With many tied zero labels, highly unequal document lengths, and small score differences between systems, confidence intervals, significance tests, per-document macro results, and span-level detection metrics are important. Padding or truncating malformed LLM outputs may also distort correlations and should be accompanied by failure-aware scoring.

Several reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous, including random seeds and variance across fine-tuning runs, exact model/API versions and dates, complete preprocessing and segmentation procedures, and the transformation between the paper's difference-oriented 0–5 labels and the similarity-oriented prompts. The manuscript's code and data links are blank in the submitted version.

Dataset accounting appears inconsistent: 224 four-language multi-parallel documents should yield 896 texts, not the reported 886. The paper should reconcile this discrepancy and state whether every document truly has all four language versions.

The resource covers only closely related, high-resource European languages in one governmental domain. This limitation is acknowledged, but it constrains the broader generality of conclusions about cross-lingual document-level RSD. Overall, the dataset is promising, but stronger validation and evaluation analysis are needed before there is a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored NLP problem: locating fine-grained semantic discrepancies in long, cross-lingual document pairs. The governmental-document setting is realistic and practically relevant.

SwissGov-RSD is potentially valuable as a naturalistic complement to synthetic, sentence-derived RSD benchmarks. It covers three language pairs, 224 multi-parallel documents, and substantially longer inputs than prior evaluation data.

The authors provide unusually extensive annotation guidelines, compensate annotators appropriately, report overlap statistics, disclose replacement of a poor annotation run, and analyze performance against individual annotators.

The empirical coverage is broad, including unsupervised alignment methods, long-context multilingual encoders, prompted and fine-tuned LLMs, projected-label training, a second rank-correlation metric, and efficiency measurements.
The main descriptive result—that performance on this dataset is much lower than on iSTS-RSD—is consistently visible across many model families.
weaknesses: The benchmark's gold-label reliability is not yet convincing. Most documents receive only one annotation, while the small doubly annotated subset shows low boundary agreement (token F1 roughly 33–56) and token-level Spearman agreement of only 0.44–0.65. Results against the two individual annotators can differ substantially—for example, EN–FR DiffAlign changes from 0.015 to 0.172—so the paper's dismissal of both values as simply “low” does not address evaluation instability or model-ranking reliability.

The evaluation metric is inadequately justified for this highly imbalanced structured task. A single token-level rank correlation mixes detection, boundary selection, and severity ranking, apparently aggregates many zero labels, and is reported without confidence intervals or significance tests. Span-level detection scores, per-document macro results, severity agreement conditional on matched spans, and uncertainty estimates are needed.

Essential score transformations and token mappings are unclear. SwissGov labels use 0 for equivalence and 5 for maximal difference, whereas the LLM prompt uses 5 for equivalence and 0 for no relation. The paper does not explicitly explain inversion before evaluation. Likewise, it does not specify how model subwords are mapped to whitespace-token annotations. These omissions impede verification of the central results.

Malformed LLM outputs are padded or truncated, but the padding value and alignment procedure are unspecified. This can strongly penalize later tokens when an earlier item is omitted and may partly produce the claimed end-of-document deterioration. Out-of-range predictions are also retained without a principled treatment. Consequently, the strong conclusion that LLMs are intrinsically limited on the task is not adequately supported.

The synthetic-versus-naturalistic comparison is heavily confounded. The datasets simultaneously differ in domain, document length, prevalence and distribution of labels, annotation process, alignment structure, and which language sides are labeled. The experiments establish a transfer gap but do not isolate natural occurrence as its cause, making claims that synthetic augmentation “fails to imitate real-world scenarios” too strong.

Model comparison is not fully controlled: short-context encoders receive an insufficiently described segmentation treatment, only selected LLMs are evaluated on SwissGov based on iSTS performance, training-set sizes differ substantially across model classes, and no repeated runs or random-seed variation are reported.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete, including random seeds, exact preprocessing and document segmentation, API model snapshots, aggregation of correlations, early-stopping specifics, and the construction of validation/test samples. The manuscript also displays blank code/data locations, so artifact availability cannot be verified from the submitted version.

There are signs of insufficient consistency checking: 224 four-language documents should yield 896 texts, not the reported 886, and some model names or parameter counts are inconsistent across tables. These are individually minor but compound the ambiguity in the experimental specification.

Overall, the resource has promise, but unresolved annotation validity and evaluation-protocol ambiguities prevent a clear Findings recommendation. A next-cycle revision could become publishable by adjudicating or multiply annotating more data, specifying and validating every label/token transformation, adding appropriate span- and document-level metrics with uncertainty, and tempering causal claims about naturalistic data.

strengths: The manuscript introduces a relevant and potentially valuable NLP resource: a naturalistic, document-level benchmark with human token-level annotations covering 224 multilingual Swiss-government documents and three English-centered language pairs. This addresses a meaningful gap left by synthetic, sentence-level RSD benchmarks. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/243ff385431d4e56a2b52aa4312b9cd0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The central empirical finding is well supported at a coarse level: every evaluated model family performs substantially worse on SwissGov-RSD than on iSTS-RSD, with gaps too large to be explained by modest implementation variation. This convincingly demonstrates that performance on the synthetic benchmark transfers poorly to natural documents.

The evaluation has useful breadth, including unsupervised alignment, prompted and fine-tuned LLMs, fine-tuned encoders, multiple model scales, projected multilingual labels, three language pairs, and both Spearman and Kendall correlations.

The paper documents data collection, annotator qualifications and compensation, guidelines, overlap checks, label distributions, model hyperparameters, prompts, and a manual audit of projected labels. The discussion is generally candid about language coverage and annotation consistency.

The benchmark is clearly relevant to multilingual content synchronization, translation evaluation, and interpretable semantic comparison. The result that inexpensive unsupervised encoders outperform specialized LLM-based approaches on naturalistic documents is practically informative.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability is the principal limitation. On the overlapping documents, token-level inter-annotator Spearman correlations are only 0.44–0.65, mean span IoU is approximately 0.24–0.44, and EN–DE annotators differ markedly in the number of identified spans. Most documents receive only one annotation, while overlap cases are resolved by selecting one annotation based partly on conformity with other annotators' label distributions rather than by independent adjudication. This makes the benchmark useful but weakens its status as authoritative gold data.

The annotator-discrepancy analysis does not cleanly establish robustness because Table 7 is mostly computed on different documents for the two annotators. Differences there confound annotator behavior with document difficulty; evaluation against both annotations on the shared subset would be more probative.

Reproducibility-critical transformations are underspecified. The human labels use 0 for equivalence and 1–5 for increasing difference, whereas the LLM prompt uses 5 for equivalence, 0 for no relation, and -1 for punctuation. The paper does not clearly explain conversion of predictions into the evaluation scale, handling of punctuation, or aggregation between model subword tokens and the whitespace-token gold annotations. Segmentation for 512-token encoders is also insufficiently described.

Correlation alone is an incomplete evaluation of token-level difference recognition under severe class imbalance. Span/token precision, recall, F1, or precision-recall metrics and document-level macro results would better reveal whether systems actually locate differences. Confidence intervals, significance tests, and variation across fine-tuning runs are absent.

Several interpretive claims outrun the experiments. The apparent advantage of segmentation is confounded with encoder architecture because there is no controlled split-versus-full-context ablation. Figure 5 analyzes token position with sharply changing sample sizes but is discussed as evidence about document length, without uncertainty estimates. Likewise, unequal training budgets—560 augmentations for LLMs versus 10,000 for encoders—limit model-family comparisons.

The evaluation of LLMs on SwissGov-RSD is selective for computational reasons and omits some of the strongest prompted systems from the synthetic benchmark. Consequently, broad claims about the limitations of current LLMs should be qualified. Dataset accounting also needs clarification: 224 genuinely four-way parallel documents would yield 896 texts, whereas the paper reports 886. These issues prevent a confident main-conference recommendation, although the core resource and synthetic-to-natural performance-gap finding appear sound enough for Findings.
